title: Why diversified rare earth supply needs a price premium
gist: Benchmark argues rare earth projects must be valued on their specific basket — DyTb for heavies, PrNd for lights — not on headline TREO. Its Q2 2026 cost curves conclude a $110/kg PrNd floor makes light rare earth projects viable without a premium, while most ex-China heavy rare earth projects stay uneconomic unless a sustained ex-China DyTb premium persists; convergence with Chinese domestic prices would collapse the diversification investment case.

themes.theme: TREO is the wrong valuation metric

insights.claim: Evaluating rare earth project economics on total rare earth oxide (TREO) alone obscures the specific commodities that actually determine commercial viability.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Screening juniors on headline TREO grade or tonnage systematically misprices them; basket composition is the real variable.
insights.quote: Evaluating project economics solely on total rare earth oxide (TREO) can therefore obscure the commodities that determine commercial viability.
insights.locator: Not all rare earth tonnes are equal.

insights.claim: Heavy rare earth projects should be assessed against dysprosium and terbium (DyTb) prices while light rare earth projects should be evaluated on praseodymium-neodymium (PrNd) oxide exposure.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Two distinct price decks to model against; conflating them produces wrong NPVs for both project classes.
insights.quote: Heavy rare earth projects should be assessed against dysprosium and terbium (DyTb) prices, whilst light rare earth projects should be evaluated on their praseodymium-neodymium (PrNd) oxide exposure.
insights.locator: Not all rare earth tonnes are equal.

insights.claim: Benchmark added cost curves to the Q2 2026 Rare Earths Forecast that compare projects only within their own peer group and stress-test publicly announced price floors against long-term price assumptions.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Peer-group cost curves plus floor stress-testing is the tool for ranking which announced projects actually get financed.
insights.locator: For this reason, Benchmark added cost curves

themes.theme: Light rare earths survive without a premium

insights.claim: A PrNd price floor of $110/kg is assessed as both feasible and economically meaningful for light rare earth producers and project developers.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: A concrete threshold: light rare earth developers pencilling below $110/kg PrNd are the exposed cohort if floors are the only support.
insights.quote: The analysis supports a PrNd price floor of $110/kg as both feasible and economically meaningful.
insights.locator: Are PrNd price floors useful for light rare earth producers

insights.claim: Light rare earth projects can survive without an ex-China premium because large volumes of low-cost refined PrNd supply are expected to come online and push prices down.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Implies limited upside to PrNd pricing: the light rare earth trade is a cost-curve position story, not a price story.
insights.quote: Light rare earth projects can survive without a premium outside China, as large volumes of refined PrNd supply are expected to come online at low cost, putting downward pressure on prices,
insights.locator: Are PrNd price floors useful for light rare earth producers

themes.theme: Heavy rare earths need a sustained ex-China DyTb premium

insights.claim: Assuming China's supply expands broadly as expected, most ex-China heavy rare earth projects remain uneconomic at lower price levels, with even several Highly Probable projects sitting close to breakeven.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Current heavy rare earth prices will not fund a diversified supply chain, so expect either policy support or project slippage.
insights.quote: Even several Highly Probable projects sit close to breakeven.
insights.locator: Does ex-China need a premium over China for heavy rare earths?

insights.claim: The ex-China DyTb premium, not a price floor, is the economic signal required to bring new heavy rare earth capacity online.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Track the ex-China versus DDP China DyTb spread as the single most informative variable for heavy rare earth developers.
insights.quote: For heavy rare earths, however, the ex-China DyTb premium is the economic signal required to bring new capacity online.
insights.locator: The conclusion is that diversified rare earth supply is achievable

insights.claim: If ex-China DyTb prices converge with Chinese domestic levels, the investment case for new geographically diversified heavy rare earth supply largely collapses.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Convergence risk is the key downside scenario for ex-China heavy rare earth developers: a spread-compression trade, not a volume story.
insights.quote: If ex-China DyTb prices converge with Chinese domestic levels, the investment case for new, geographically diversified heavy rare earth supply largely collapses,
insights.locator: The structural challenge is therefore clearest

insights.claim: Premium compression can arrive through three distinct channels — policy intervention, excess supply, or demand destruction — and any of them would render much of the ex-China heavy rare earth pipeline unviable again.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: A three-factor risk checklist for monitoring heavy rare earth project financing risk.
insights.quote: If that premium compresses through policy intervention, excess supply, or demand destruction, much of the ex-China heavy rare earth pipeline will again become unviable.
insights.locator: The conclusion is that diversified rare earth supply is achievable

insights.claim: Ex-China heavy rare earth projects carry four structural cost disadvantages: higher energy costs, lower by-product credits, more stringent environmental requirements, and substantial greenfield capital expenditure.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: These are persistent rather than cyclical disadvantages; the cost gap will not close on its own with scale or time.
insights.quote: Ex-China projects face higher energy costs, lower by-product credits, more stringent environmental requirements, and substantial greenfield capital expenditure.
insights.locator: The structural challenge is therefore clearest

insights.claim: Applying upside long-term price assumptions that embed sustained ex-China premiums moves a significant proportion of the Probable and Highly Probable heavy rare earth pipeline from loss-making to breakeven or profitable.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Quantifies how price-elastic the ex-China pipeline is: a modest sustained premium unlocks a large tranche of supply.
insights.locator: Applying Benchmark's upside long-term price assumptions

insights.claim: A premium generated by a temporary price spike is insufficient to unlock marginal heavy rare earth supply; only a sustained premium works.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Rare earth price spikes should not be read as a supply-response trigger absent structural change.
insights.quote: The premium must be sustained, rather than generated by a temporary price spike,
insights.locator: However, this is not the only solution

insights.claim: Developers and financiers require mine-life confidence supported by durable pricing mechanisms, offtake agreements, government assistance, and credible end-user commitments before committing capital.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: A four-item due-diligence checklist for judging which announced rare earth projects will actually reach a financing decision.
insights.quote: Developers and financiers require confidence over a project’s mine life, supported by durable pricing mechanisms, offtake agreements, government assistance, and credible end-user commitments.
insights.locator: However, this is not the only solution
